summary.text: 多 means “many” or “much.” Early inscriptional contexts already use it for “many.” The graph’s original motivation is unsettled: early forms are analyzed as two 肉 (flesh) shapes, but whether they suggested abundance or conveyed “many” through repetition is disputed.

formation.text: The reported early graph is described as two 肉-like forms, so a pictographic compound is a supported account of its construction. The proposed explanations differ: the forms may have pictured two pieces of meat to suggest abundance, or repetition may have conveyed “many.” Neither motivation is settled. The later-looking 夕+夕 analysis in the Shuowen is a separate historical explanation, not proof of the earliest construction.

components.text: In the reported early form, 肉 depicts flesh. One of two such shapes is analyzed as part of 多; its specific contribution to the meaning is uncertain because the graph’s original motivation is disputed. Later forms came to resemble 夕.

This is the proposed second 肉-like pictorial element in the early analysis. It may have contributed to an image of abundant meat, or its repetition may have conveyed “many”; a one-肉 personal-name form complicates the doubling account.

history.text: The curated oracle-script illustration is a modern redraw of an early form. It illustrates the form discussed in the two-肉 analysis but cannot by itself settle the shapes’ identity or the graph’s original motivation.

Later bronze and bamboo forms are reported to have become visually confused with 夕, though a 肉-like shape persisted in a bronze form of the 多 component in 宜. The precise timing of this graphic change is unresolved. The Shuowen’s analysis as 重 plus 夕 is a separate historical explanation.

uncertainties.text: The original motivation remains unsettled. Two pieces of meat suggesting abundance and repetition conveying “many” are competing proposals; a one-肉 personal-name form complicates a simple doubling explanation.

Early inscriptions support the meaning “many,” but the cited oracle-bone example has no exact date established here. The available attestations and dictionary glosses do not establish a complete chronology for later senses.

evidence.text: Two nights 夕, suggesting many
Pictograph of two identical objects to convey the meaning "many". Not related to 夕 (dusk).
重也。从重夕。夕者，相繹也，故爲多。重夕爲多，重日爲曡。凡多之屬皆从多。

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意) – two pieces of meat (肉). In the bronze script, 肉 was corrupted into 夕 due to visual similarity, making 多 into a duplication of 夕. The form with 夕 was inherited in later scripts.
Chi (2010) suggests that meat is scarce in ancient times, so two pieces of meat is a lot, citing a passage from Mencius:
:
Chang Ping-chuan suggests that it is the duplicative nature of the character that gives the meaning of "many", just like in 林 (“forest”), from 木 (“tree; wood”).
Etymology unclear. Schuessler (2007) suggests that it is in the same word family as 諸 (OC *tjaː, *tja, “many; all”) and 庶 (OC *hljaɡs, “many”).
Hill (2014, 2019) compares it to Tibetan ཆེ (che, “big”), མཐེ་བོ (mthe bo, “thumb”), Burmese တယ် (tai, “very”). STEDT derives the latter two from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ta-j (“big”), whose Chinese comparandum is 大 (OC *daːds, “large”) instead; Baxter (1992) has also compared it to this etymon.
Baxter and Sagart (1998) propose that there may be a prefix *t- in this word that gives a mass noun reading, which may nullify the connection to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ta-j (“big”). However, Baxter and Sagart (2014) may have withdrawn from this theory since they no longer indicate the *t as a prefix.
Also compare Proto-Tai *ʰlaːjᴬ (“many, much”), whence Thai หลาย (lǎai, “many”) and Zhuang lai (“many”), and Proto-Hlai *hləːy (“many”) (Gong Qunhu, 2002; Schuessler, 2007; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). Schuessler (2007) considers the Chinese word to be from Kra-Dai, but others suggest that the direction of borrowing may have been the other way (Li, 1977; Baxter and Sagart, 1998; Norquest, 2007).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database, CUHK）
evidence.field: 形義通解；古文字字形、用例
evidence.text: The database displays oracle-bone, bronze, bamboo-slip and small-seal forms. Its account says oracle-bone 多 is formed from two 肉 shapes; later bronze and bamboo forms were confused with 夕. It reports the graph used with the sense ‘many’, opposed to 少, in oracle-bone and bronze examples: 《合集》12496 多雨 and the inscription on the 不其簋 多禽（擒）. It also cites Warring States and Qin-slip uses. These examples support an early ‘many’ reading, while the database itself says the graph’s original motivation is uncertain: the two-meat explanation and an analogy with 林 are proposals, and a personal-name form written with one 肉 is cited against a simple doubling explanation.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 字頭「多」

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database, CUHK）
evidence.text: The database describes 肉 as a pictograph of animal flesh and separately gives oracle-bone examples of 肉 used for flesh. For 多 it reports two 肉 forms in oracle-bone writing, with later component shapes merging visually with 夕. The claim that two pieces of meat convey ‘many’ is attributed to 季旭昇; the database also presents 張秉權’s comparison to 林 from two 木, then notes a one-meat variant in the name 帚(婦)多 as counterevidence. Its conclusion is that 多’s original graph motivation is unsettled. Its discussion of component discrimination says the ordinary bronze 多 form visually matches 夕, whereas the 多 component retained in bronze 宜 forms resembles 肉.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 肉部字形及「多」相關條目

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫（Chinese Character Database, CUHK）
evidence.text: The page transmits the Shuowen explanation “重也。从重夕。夕者，相繹也，故爲多” and identifies 得何切; it gives the Guangyun fanqie 得何, level tone, 果攝歌韻, open mouth, first division. The database lists Mandarin pronunciation but provides no phonetic-component analysis for 多. This Shuowen account is a historical lexicographic explanation, not independent proof that the graph was originally two 夕.

evidence.source: Kotobank, citing Heibonsha 普及版 字通
evidence.text: This dictionary presents the character as 夕＋夕 while explaining that 夕 represents 肉 here, and takes 多 as ‘many meat’ or abundant sacrificial meat. It reports extensions including ‘many/abundant’, ‘surpass’, ‘excess’, and ‘praise/esteem’. This is a dictionary’s interpretation; the more cautious CUHK account identifies uncertainty about whether the earliest graph’s motivation was meat or duplication.

It lists senses including ‘many’, ‘surpass’, ‘excess’, and ‘praise/esteem’, and reports older gloss traditions. This is a dictionary account; the inspected CUHK discussion leaves the earliest motivation unresolved, and these listed senses do not by themselves establish their chronology or semantic links.
evidence.title: コトバンク — 普及版 字通「多」

evidence.source: 文音聲韻查詢系統, reporting 廣韻
evidence.text: The entry reports 多 as 得何切, 端母, 歌一韻, 平聲. This is a Middle Chinese rhyme-book classification; the page does not provide evidence of a phonetic component within 多.
evidence.title: 「多」字的廣韻切語及中古讀音

evidence.source: 小學堂字形演變資料庫 — Academia Sinica
evidence.field: 字形演變、解形與 rights status
evidence.text: The inspected page displays labeled categories for oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo/silk, small-seal and Shuowen forms and repeats competing explanations of two 夕 components versus 夕 as meat. Its footer states All Rights Reserved. No asset from this site is proposed for reuse; the official Xiaoxuetang single-character query returned HTTP 401 in the supplied query result.
evidence.title: 漢字「多」：字形演變

evidence.field: File description, source provenance and license
evidence.text: The file page identifies 多-oracle.svg as a depiction of 多 in Shang oracle script style, says its source references include the Academia Sinica database and Hanziyuan, and points to Hanziyuan record J16735 for this drawing. The file is a modern Inkscape SVG redraw, not an artifact photograph. Its page states a public-domain release for the SVG representation. The original-file endpoint was identified on the page but the web tool failed to fetch the image binary.
evidence.title: File:多-oracle.svg

evidence.field: Original file URL and access result
evidence.text: The Commons file page links the original SVG at this URL; opening it failed with a cache-miss error. The page itself was inspected and supplied the file identity and rights statement, but this research did not inspect the rendered pixels.
evidence.kind: direct image candidate; binary fetch failed
evidence.title: 多-oracle.svg original file

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: site:ctext.org 多 說文解字 許慎 重也; 多 得何切 廣韻 字源
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the Shuowen text and a Guangyun-based phonological entry. These confirm the historical lexicographic account and reported Middle Chinese classification, not an original component sound role.

gaps: The CUHK page gives inventory counts and links to oracle-bone and bronze images, but this research did not inspect those images or identify individual vessels and palaeographic dates. The attestations support early use of 多 for ‘many’, but no exact date for the cited oracle-bone item or 不其簋 inscription was established here.

The graph’s original motivation remains unresolved in the consulted source: the meat interpretation is proposed, the duplication interpretation is also discussed, and the one-meat personal-name variant complicates both. No independently inspected primary facsimile or specialist monograph was available to adjudicate these proposals.

The available evidence supports later graphic resemblance to 夕 and a reported early two-肉 form; it does not establish a specific dated moment of corruption or a complete graphic sequence. Shuowen’s two-夕 account is recorded as its own historical explanation, not confirmation of the earliest form.

No phonetic component or whole-graph phonetic loan claim was substantiated. Modern Mandarin and Guangyun categories were checked on the CUHK page, but a primary Baxter–Sagart entry for 多 could not be inspected; the dossier’s reconstructed forms remain unverified in this research.

The database cites both ‘many’/abundance and an adverbial or frequentative use in early texts, but exact textual dates and a fully documented pathway for senses such as ‘more than’, ‘surpass’, ‘too/excessively’, or ‘praise/esteem’ were not established. These should not be ordered chronologically from modern dictionary glosses.
No semantic borrowing history or cross-language word-family claim (including proposed Tai/Kra-Dai relationships in the dossier excerpt) was independently examined or verified.
The earliest graph’s motivation remains unsettled in the inspected paleographic account: the two-meat and duplication analyses are proposals, and a one-meat personal-name variant complicates them.

The proposed transition from early 肉-like forms to later forms visually read as 夕 is supported as a reported graphic development, but no dated sequence or precise point of graphic conflation was established here. The transmitted Shuowen account of 重夕 is a separate historical explanation.

The early ‘many’ sense is supported by oracle-bone contexts including 《合集》12496, but no exact date for that individual inscription was established. The broadly Late Shang corpus dating is contextual only. The cited Warring States adverbial use does not establish a full semantic chronology.

Dictionary-listed extensions such as ‘surpass’, ‘excess’, and ‘praise/esteem’ were not traced to dated attestations or linked through a documented semantic pathway. No full chronology should be inferred from the gloss list.

No sound component or whole-graph phonetic loan claim was substantiated. Modern Mandarin and Guangyun evidence are available, but no component role is independently proposed, so there is no second character reading to compare phonologically.
The Xiaoxuetang per-character query was unavailable (HTTP 401 in supplied query data), and its rights notice page did not expose readable text during inspection. No Xiaoxuetang image was selected.

The proposed Commons glyph is documented and its modern redraw and public-domain status are described on the source page, but the direct file binary could not be fetched in this research stage; its pixels were not inspected.

items.period: Shang oracle script style; file page does not specify a narrower date
items.caption: A modern redraw of an oracle-script form of 多. Early forms are reported as two 肉-like shapes, though the character’s original graphic motivation remains uncertain.
items.alt: Black oracle-script-style form of 多, drawn as two stacked, box-like shapes with open left sides and vertical strokes near the right.
items.selection_reason: This legible candidate illustrates the early graphic form relevant to accounts of two 肉-like components and the character’s early use for “many.” The shape alone cannot settle the components’ identity or the graph’s original motivation.
items.rights: Public domain release for the SVG representation, as stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: The earliest graph’s motivation is unresolved: explanations involving two pieces of meat or graphic duplication are proposals, and a one-meat personal-name variant complicates them.
The early ‘many’ use is reported in oracle-bone contexts, but the cited inscription has no established exact date here; no dated sequence establishes when the forms came to resemble 夕.
